d01.title: Where to Base
d01.sf: Where you sleep decides what kind of trip you have — because “central” in Barcelona means three incompatible things, and the mistake is picking the one whose character is wrong for your days.
d01.caption: The base decision, by traveller · first-timer, 3–5 days
rows: the default: central, calm at night, deepest hotel stock, Gaudí on your walking route ◈
medieval lanes, bars, the Picasso; central but lively after dark ◈
sand and boardwalk; Poblenou calmer and more local ◈
real prices, excellent eating, below Montjuïc; a metro hop from the core ◈
d01.strong: First trip, no special agenda: the Eixample, and it isn't close.
d01.rest: Central, quiet at night, deepest hotel stock, and it puts Gaudí's front doors on your walking route. Choose El Born only if atmosphere is the point and you sleep through noise; choose the beach only if you will actually be at the beach rather than commuting from it. Most first-timers who override the default are solving for a preference they do not really have.

d02.title: The Apartment Question
d02.sf: If you would book an apartment the way you would in any other city — stop. Barcelona is eliminating tourist apartments entirely, and the naive move has quietly become the risky one.
d02.caption: The apartment call, by traveller · inside the phase-out
rows: licence anxiety and a possible pulled booking, for a kitchen you won't use in three days ◈
you want space and a kitchen, but the pull-risk is identical ◈
unlicensed listings that vanish; direct-transfer hosts with no recourse ◇
d02.strong: For most American first-timers in this climate, the honest call is a hotel or an apart-hotel — not the apartment.
d02.rest: What is left of the licensed market is pricier, books earlier, and sits in a pool increasingly padded with listings that should not exist. If you want a kitchen, the apart-hotel buys the feel without the licence roulette. Reserve the true apartment for when you have a valid HUTB number and real payment protection.

d03.title: The Money-Trap Web
d03.sf: No single one of these will ruin your trip — which is exactly why they work. The city takes your money in four small bites, in four places, and counts on you never seeing the pattern. Here it is, in one place.
d03.caption: The four extractions, and the defence · per couple, five days
rows: The tourist tax you didn't budget
per person, per night, on top of the room rate; rose 1 Apr 2026 ◆ and lands at check-out
T-casual and singles do not work at the airport metro ●; Hola and T-usual do
the terminal or ATM offers USD on a helpful screen ●; accept and you eat a markup ▲
The tourist ATM and tourist lunch
blue standalone machines push DCC and layer fees ●; the tourist dinner is the menú in reverse
d03.strong: The four moves take five minutes to internalise and defend the better part of a couple's discretionary week.
d03.rest: Budget the bed tax so it cannot surprise you, buy the right airport ticket in both directions, say “euros” at every terminal, and pull cash from a bank machine. None of this is exotic and none of it needs an app — it needs knowing the four gates exist before you reach them. That is the entire edge: the charges are public, the pattern is not.

d05.title: Sequencing the Days
d05.sf: Most itineraries treat the days as interchangeable boxes. They are not — three of the things you will do are time-locked in ways that collide, and slotting them wrong costs you the good version of each sight rather than the sight itself.
d05.caption: The time-locked pieces, and where they belong · five days
rows: the nave gold at 9:00–9:30, ahead of the crush ▲
booked midday: the crush and the flattest light
jet-lag-proof: old-city wander, early dinner, nothing timed ◈
a ticket you are too fried to use
The day trip → a full clear day
Montserrat or Girona get the day they need ◈
wedged into a morning: a commute with a view
moved to whichever afternoon turns warm ◈
pinned to a grey Thursday; never happens
d05.strong: Anchor three things and let everything else flow around them:
d05.rest: Sagrada Família on a morning slot, the day trip on a full clear day mid-trip so a grey forecast can still be traded, and the beach kept deliberately unpinned. Arrival day holds nothing timed. Do this and every sight lands in its good version; skip it and you will technically see everything while getting the lesser cut of half of it. The order is the product here — the list is free on the blog.

d06.title: The Gaudí Fork
d06.sf: Barcelona sells you a dozen Gaudí doors and implies you should walk through all of them. You should not — and the reason is attention rather than money. Three interiors in two days and the fourth is wallpaper.
d06.caption: The Gaudí sites, ranked by what earns a ticket · first trip
rows: the nave; the one building unlike any you have seen ◈
the mosaic terrace and the city view; timed and slotted ◈
One house: Batlló or La Pedrera
one dazzling interior and a rooftop; one is plenty ◈
façades, enjoyable without the ticket queue ◈
d06.strong: Two ticketed Gaudí sites and one house is the first-timer's sweet spot:
d06.rest: Sagrada Família in the morning, Park Güell on your slot, and exactly one of Casa Batlló or La Pedrera. That is a full, un-saturated dose. Everything else folds into the walks between them. The saturation trap costs attention and money at once — the fourth interior you paid for is the one you barely see.

d07.title: Which Day Trip
d07.sf: The day-trip mistake is not a bad choice among the options — they are all good. It is choosing by proximity or by a photograph instead of by fit, and then spending a travel day on the wrong one for you.
d07.caption: The day trips, by fit · one day, by train from Barcelona
rows: serrated mountain, monastery, Black Madonna; FGC R5 then cable car ◈
the one to take if you take one
walled old town and the Onyar houses; fast train ◈
history walkers; cobbles, slopes and steps
resort beaches and whitewashed lanes, just south ◈
a sea day, not a sightseeing one
Tarragona — Roman ruins by the sea
amphitheatre and Roman remains on the coast ◈
d07.strong: If you take one, take Montserrat.
d07.rest: It out-memories the city for most visitors, and the mountain-plus-monastery has no substitute within reach. Swap to Girona if you would rather have a medieval city and no climbing, or Sitges if what you want is a beach day with a change of scene. Figueres and Tarragona are specialist picks — superb for the Dalí devotee or the Roman-ruins person, underwhelming if you are neither. The wrong day trip is not ruinous; it is a day spent on someone else's ideal day.

d08.title: How Not to Eat Like a Tourist
d08.sf: Barcelona is one of the great eating cities and one of the easiest to eat badly in — because the streets you will naturally walk are lined with places built for visitors who do not know the tells.
d08.caption: The four eating traps, and the rule that beats each
rows: real rice is cooked to order
tourist-register plates at tourist prices on the main drag ●
Dinner prices for what lunch does better
paying evening rates for the meal a weekday midday serves for less
eating on American time and getting the rooms that serve it ●
d08.strong: Eat the menú del día at least once, order rice where it is cooked to order, keep your tapas off the tourist spine, and eat on Spanish time.
d08.rest: That is the defence entire, and three of the four rules cost you less while feeding you better — the tourist premium here buys a worse meal, which makes this the rare trap that is easy to refuse once you can see it. The city's food reputation is entirely earned. You simply have to order out of the local register rather than the one built for you.
